pairs.rationale: John promises the hearer who believes the One who sent Jesus life without coming into judgment; Romans declares no condemnation for those in Christ. The related judgment-and-life assurance retains its different stated conditions, not an identical sentence or an added longer ending to Romans.

Both describe freedom in relation to Christ. Romans names the law of the Spirit of life setting you free from the law of sin and death; Galatians says Christ set us free and warns against a slavery yoke. The agents, pronouns and two law expressions are not collapsed.

Both describe God sending His Son with a saving purpose in relation to law and human existence. Romans specifies likeness of sinful flesh and condemnation of sin in flesh; Galatians specifies birth from a woman, law and adoption. Romans condemns sin, not an assertion that the Son personally sinned.

Both contrast walking by Spirit with fleshly desire. Romans adds fulfilment of the law's righteous requirement in such walkers; Galatians adds being led by Spirit and not being under law. The different law clauses and the respective conditions remain intact.

Both contrast the objects on which people set their minds. Romans names flesh and Spirit; Colossians names things above, where Christ is, and things on earth. The paired orientations correspond without defining every earthly thing as identical with Romans' flesh.

Romans contrasts the fleshly mind's death with the Spirit's life and peace; Galatians contrasts reaping corruption from flesh with eternal life from Spirit. The opposed outcomes correspond, with mind versus sowing imagery and peace stated only in Romans.

Colossians describes former alienation and hostility in mind in evil deeds, followed by reconciliation; Romans describes the fleshly mind's hostility and failure to submit to God's law. The mind-and-hostility language corresponds, without inserting Romans' incapacity clause into Colossians or erasing its subsequent reconciliation.

Both state an inability to please God under a specified condition. Romans names being in flesh; Hebrews names absence of faith and explains approaching God. The conditions are compared, not rewritten as identical definitions or a claim that a physical body itself excludes pleasing God.

Both describe the presence of God's Spirit in the addressed community. Romans says dwells in you and qualifies belonging to Christ; Corinthians says dwells among you in its temple image. In/among, the conditional belonging statement and the temple image retain their respective wording.

Both describe Christ within the believer together with death/life language. Romans calls the body dead because of sin and the Spirit life because of righteousness; Galatians describes dying to law, crucifixion with Christ and Christ living in me. The objects and explanations of death are not made identical.

Both connect God's raising the Lord/Christ with future life for believers. Romans names mortal bodies and the indwelling Spirit through whom life is given; Corinthians names God's power. The selected Corinthian verse does not independently repeat the Spirit-dwelling condition or call the Spirit the resurrected person.

Romans denies an obligation to live according to flesh; Galatians describes those belonging to Christ crucifying fleshly passions and keeping in step with Spirit. Both reject flesh as the governing way of life, with debt and crucifixion as different images rather than a specified financial debt.

Both speak of putting to death disordered bodily conduct. Romans states conditional life/death alternatives and names acting by Spirit; Colossians directly commands putting to death earthly members and lists vices. The objects and grammatical forms remain distinct, without making either text a direction literally to destroy the person's body.

Both explicitly describe being led by Spirit. Romans draws the conclusion sons of God; Galatians draws not under law. The shared guidance expression does not make those conclusions word-for-word identical or add an unprinted adoption statement to Galatians5:18.

Both connect sonship, the rejection of slavery and Abba, Father with the Spirit. Romans says we cry in the Spirit; Galatians describes God sending His Son's Spirit into our hearts, crying the address. The crying subjects and the sending/adoption formulations remain distinct.

Both link the Spirit's presence with being God's sons or children. Romans describes the Spirit witnessing with our spirit; Galatians gives sonship as the reason for God sending His Son's Spirit into our hearts. Witnessing and crying are not made identical actions.

Both explicitly reason from being a child/son to being an heir. Romans additionally names joint inheritance with Christ and suffering toward shared glory; Galatians contrasts former slavery and heirship through God. The selected Galatians verse does not independently supply those suffering-and-glory qualifications.

Both compare present affliction with a far greater glory. Corinthians uses the momentary lightness and eternal weight comparison and seen/unseen language; Romans speaks of sufferings now and glory to be revealed in us. The descriptions and temporal contrasts correspond without identifying every hardship or date.

Romans anticipates the revealing of God's sons, and Colossians promises that the addressed people will be revealed with Christ in glory when He is revealed. The future manifestation corresponds, while creation's eager waiting is Romans' own description and Christ's revelation is expressly named in Colossians.

Genesis describes the earth cursed in Adam's labors, painful toil and return to earth; Romans describes creation subjected unwillingly to futility in hope. The curse-and-frustration account supplies possible background, without making the earth passage an identical statement about the extent of creation or reproducing Romans' hope clause.

Both look toward a future condition of the created order. Romans describes creation freed from corruption into the children's glorious freedom; Peter awaits new heavens and earth where righteousness dwells. Liberation and new-creation descriptions remain different, without inserting Peter's surrounding fire imagery or an exact process into Romans.

The next not-only-but-also sentence explicitly joins the believers' inward groaning to creation's groaning here. The actors and images remain distinct: creation labors in birth pangs, while the believers await bodily redemption with the Spirit's firstfruits. This is an internal connection, not independent testimony.

Both describe groaning toward a life-giving bodily future and a present gift of the Spirit. Romans names adoption, bodily redemption and firstfruits; Corinthians uses heavenly clothing, mortality swallowed by life and the Spirit's pledge. The metaphors and particular formulations are not made identical.

Both relate expectation to what is not seen. Romans explains why seen hope would not be hope; Hebrews describes faith as assurance of hoped-for things and conviction of unseen realities. The correspondence does not erase the distinction between faith and hope or turn them into one verbatim definition.

Romans joins waiting for unseen hope with perseverance; Hebrews calls for endurance to receive the promise and anticipates the coming One. The endurance-and-future-expectation relation corresponds, without inserting the coming quotation's little-while wording into Romans or assigning an exact interval.

This chapter describes intercession by both the Spirit and Christ Jesus. Here the Spirit helps weakness and intercedes with groanings beyond words; the later verse names the dead-and-raised Christ at God's right hand. The related intercession roles do not identify the Spirit as the crucified person or give Christ this verse's groanings.

Romans names the One searching hearts who knows the Spirit's mind; Jeremiah has the Lord examine hearts and test kidneys before rendering according to conduct. The divine heart-examination language corresponds, while Jeremiah does not independently state the Spirit's intercession or its according-to-God clause.

Joseph distinguishes his brothers' intended evil from God's intended good that many might be fed; Romans speaks of all things working together for good for God-lovers called according to purpose. The providential-good comparison retains its different scope and does not declare the brothers' evil intention intrinsically good.

Romans describes predestined conformity to the Son's image; Corinthians anticipates bearing the heavenly One's image after bearing the earthly one's. The believer-transformation image corresponds, while the firstborn-among-many-brothers clause and the explicit predestination wording are not added to the Corinthian verse.

Both attribute the people's destiny to God's prior purpose. Romans sequences predestining, calling, justifying and glorifying; Ephesians names choice before the world, predestination to adoption through Jesus and glorious grace. Their acts and verb forms are not converted into one identical sequence or an added justification clause.

The psalm grounds confidence against human threat in the Lord as helper; Romans asks who can stand against those for whom God is. This is a related confidence formula, not a claim that opponents or persecution cease to exist; Romans' question has a broader stated scope than the psalm's man.

The not-sparing-a-son language closely recalls the angel's commendation of Abraham concerning his beloved son. Genesis expressly stops harm to Isaac; Romans says God did not spare His own Son but handed Him over for all. The comparison preserves that crucial difference rather than claiming Isaac was killed.

Both place a challenge to would-be accusers beside divine justification or help. Isaiah's speaker says the One justifying him draws near and challenges a case against him; Romans speaks of God justifying His chosen ones. Singular/plural, the case language and Isaiah's harm question retain their own formulations.

Both name continuing intercession by Jesus for His people. Romans places the dead-and-raised Christ at God's right hand; Hebrews says He always lives to intercede for those approaching God through Him. The selected Hebrews verse does not itself repeat the resurrection-and-right-hand clauses or make Jesus the One approached through Himself.

The chapter's concluding assurance answers its separation question with a further list of things unable to separate from God's love in Christ. The hardship list and cosmic list differ, and Christ's love here and God's love in Christ there keep their actual formulations. These are connected stages of one argument.

Paul explicitly cites the communal lament's all-day death and sheep-for-slaughter wording. The retained psalm closely matches the quotation, without identifying its original sufferers with every Roman addressee or making it a separate historical report of the current hardship list.

Both locate victory through the Lord rather than unaided human strength. Romans describes more-than-conquering amid the listed afflictions through the One who loved us; Corinthians thanks God for victory through Jesus in its death/resurrection argument. The circumstances and love clause are not made identical.

Paul's list of rulers, powers and present/future threats can be compared with Christ raised and seated above every rule, authority and power in this age and the coming one. The authority-and-time descriptions correspond, without equating the lists or adding Romans' whole love-separation conclusion to Ephesians.

Romans denies any created thing power to separate from God's love in Christ; Jesus promises His sheep life and no snatching from His or the Father's hand. The protective assurance is comparable, while love/separation and sheep/hands are different images. John's what-the-Father-gave clause is not rewritten with Father as its grammatical subject.

Both appeals invoke conscience as witness to the speaker's conduct or truthfulness. Romans adds speaking in Christ and witness in the Holy Spirit; Corinthians names simplicity and sincerity from God and God's grace. The stated grounds differ and neither appeal is an independent audit of every prior action.

Both describe anguish of heart in Paul's concern for others. Romans calls it great and unceasing; Corinthians describes a letter written through affliction and tears to make love known. The circumstances, duration and recipients remain distinct rather than one identical grief episode.

Moses offers to be blotted from God's book if the people's sin is not forgiven; Paul says he could wish to be accursed away from Christ for his fleshly kinsmen. The self-sacrificial intercession motif corresponds, without treating either conditional appeal as a narrated actual exclusion or equating book and Christ as identical terms.

The Lord's designation of Israel as His firstborn son supplies a concrete corporate-sonship background for the Israelites' adoption in Romans. It does not independently repeat the whole privileges list, or turn firstborn into a statement of literal divine biological parentage.

Both identify the Christ's human ancestry using according-to-the-flesh language. The opening names David's seed; this passage names Israel's fathers and adds its God-blessed doxological clause. The latter clause is retained in Romans9 rather than represented as part of the selected opening verse.

Both distinguish a qualifying identity beyond outward status alone. Romans9 contrasts being from Israel with being Israel; Romans2 contrasts outward and inward Jew and fleshly and heart circumcision. These related distinctions are not forced into identical definitions or a modern civil classification.

Romans quotes the Isaac-seed-called declaration spoken by God to Abraham. Genesis places it within the Sarah, child and slave-woman exchange and also promises a nation for the other son. Those fuller family circumstances are not erased or made additional words in the short quotation.

Both use Isaac and promise to explain the identity of children. Romans contrasts fleshly children with children reckoned as promise-seed; Galatians directly addresses its hearers as children of promise like Isaac. The applications and exact predicates differ rather than supplying one identical genealogy.

The return-at-the-appointed-season and Sarah-having-a-son declaration corresponds to the promise in the Genesis conversation. Romans shortens it to at-this-time I will come; Genesis says return when the season comes round and includes Sarah's response. The wording and fuller scene remain distinct.

Genesis names Isaac and Rebekah, her conception and the twins; Romans introduces Rebecca's conception by one man, Isaac. This connects the named family and pregnancy, while the one-man emphasis and subsequent election argument are not treated as a separate Genesis quotation or independent biological investigation.

Genesis places the oracle while the children are still within Rebekah, before its narrated birth. That supplies the prebirth setting for Paul's argument; the explicit good-or-bad-works and election-purpose clauses belong to Romans, not an extra moral assessment of the unborn children's leaping in Genesis.

Paul's older-will-serve-younger citation corresponds to Genesis's greater-will-serve-lesser oracle. The target explicitly names two nations and peoples in the womb. Its comparative wording and national setting are preserved rather than silently changed to Paul's age terms or a narrated personal enslavement of Esau.

The Jacob-loved/Esau-hated wording is directly present in Malachi. Its setting addresses Israel and continues into territorial desolation and Idumea; Romans uses the citation in its election argument. The comparison does not invent a new prebirth speech or substitute later territorial details for the quoted persons.

The Song declares a faithful God with no unrighteousness, corresponding to Paul's rejection of unrighteousness with God. The shared assertion concerns divine justice, with song declaration and argumentative question/answer as different forms rather than an unprinted explanation of every election claim.

Paul reproduces the divine mercy-and-compassion formula spoken in the reply to Moses' request for glory. The quoted selection corresponds closely, while the preceding passing-in-glory and proclamation-of-the-name words remain in Exodus rather than being added to Romans.

Both contrast human performance with God's mercy. Romans denies willing/running as its determining basis; Titus says salvation is not on the basis of righteous works done by us but according to mercy. The particular actions and Titus's washing/Spirit-renewal description remain distinct.

Both connect Pharaoh's continued position with demonstration of divine power and proclamation of God's name throughout the earth. Romans says I raised you up; the supplied Exodus says you were preserved. The shared purpose is retained without replacing that passive preservation wording or naming an unprinted Pharaoh.

The Lord explicitly hardens Pharaoh's heart in Exodus, supplying a particular instance for Paul's hardening conclusion. The mercy half of Romans' summary draws on the preceding argument rather than appearing in this Exodus verse; the named hardening agent is not changed to Pharaoh alone.

Paul voices an imagined objection about resisted purpose and continued fault; Wisdom asks who can oppose God's judgment or confront Him. The divine-authority questions correspond, but their argumentative roles differ and Wisdom is not made the speaker of Paul's whole objection or an endorsement of its premise.

Both picture the formed thing addressing its former. Isaiah's object denies its formation or the maker's intelligence; Romans asks why it was made this way. The maker/object challenge corresponds, while the quoted questions are not word-for-word identical.

Wisdom depicts a human potter deciding uses of vessels from the same clay, for clean and opposite purposes; Romans uses potter/clay authority and vessels for honor or dishonor. This is concrete craft-image background, not a claim that Wisdom supplies Paul's whole election argument or that its ensuing idol-maker charge describes God.

Both speak of divine patience beside the prospect of destruction. Romans describes enduring wrath-vessels fitted for destruction; Peter describes the Lord's patience toward you and desire for repentance rather than perishing. The objects and purposes differ, and the unspecified fitting agent in Romans is not supplied from the next verse.

Both place divine riches and mercy within God's saving action toward His people. Romans names prepared mercy-vessels and glory; Ephesians names God rich in mercy, life with Christ and future display of rich grace. The preparation clause and vessel image are not inserted into Ephesians or every action assigned to Christ instead of God.

The opening Jew/Gentile question includes both groups under the one God's justifying action; this passage includes both in those called. The same two-group scope corresponds, while calling and justifying remain different predicates and the circumcision formulations are not made exact ethnic definitions for every person.

Hosea says to Not My People, You are My people, and shows mercy to Not Shown Mercy; Paul says call not-my-people My people and not-beloved beloved. The restoration reversal corresponds, but say/call and mercy/beloved are actual differences, not silently normalized wording. Hosea's own restored-people setting remains distinct from Paul's Jews-and-Gentiles application.

The in-that-place reversal from Not My People to sons of the living God closely matches Hosea's declaration. The fuller target first names Israel's sons like sea sand and then the restored title; that first sentence is not inserted into this shorter citation or converted into an independent list of Paul's addressees.

Both combine Israel's sea-sand multitude with a remnant being saved. Romans names the number of Israel's sons and introduces Isaiah's cry; Isaiah names Israel's people and continues into the shortened word. The size description does not erase the remnant distinction or independently count either population.

The completing-and-shortening word corresponds to Isaiah's completed/shortened word. Romans names the Lord carrying it out on earth; Isaiah adds in righteousness and the whole inhabited world. Those fuller clauses are not restored from another edition to lengthen the supplied short Romans verse.

The Lord Sabaoth leaving seed and the resulting contrast with Sodom and Gomorrah closely match the retained Isaiah wording. Paul explicitly introduces the prior saying; neither text's seed is silently replaced with a different translation or an invented count of survivors.

Gentiles attaining without pursuing can be compared with the later cited declaration of God being found among non-seekers. These are internal instances of unexpected reception, while attaining righteousness by faith and finding God are different predicates and the Isaiah wording retains its own speaker.

Paul's next account of zeal without knowledge and seeking one's own righteousness develops the failure of the law pursuit stated here. The later explanation does not lengthen Romans9:31's final did-not-attain-law wording or say that every Israelite has the same response.

Both contrast faith with works in discussing righteousness or justification. Romans explains the stumbling pursuit as not from faith but as though from works; Galatians explicitly contrasts faith in Christ with works of law. The different qualifying language and the stone image remain in their respective passages.

Isaiah supplies the placing of a stone in Zion and trust without shame. Romans names a stumbling stone and says believes in Him; Isaiah names a costly chosen cornerstone and says trusts in it. The object pronoun, stone descriptions and the shortened quotation remain distinct.

The stumbling-stone/falling-rock language provides the other stone-image comparison. The supplied Isaiah condition says those trusting Him will not encounter Him in that way, then names Jacob's trap; Romans positively names a stone of stumbling and rock of offense. The imagery is compared without deleting Isaiah's condition or negation.

The desire and prayer for their salvation continue Paul's sorrow and conditional wish on behalf of fleshly kinsmen. The connection identifies his ongoing concern rather than making the earlier wish an actual curse or saying its words were the same prayer.

Paul's defense describes his own strict-law education and zeal for God together with his earlier persecution. This supplies an individual comparison for zeal not guaranteeing right knowledge, without attributing every act of his former persecution to every person in Romans' addressed group.

Philippians explicitly contrasts my own righteousness from law with righteousness from God through faith in Christ. Romans contrasts seeking their own righteousness with not submitting to God's righteousness. The own/from-God distinction corresponds, with different speakers' positions and faith stated explicitly in the target.

Both place Christ and faith at a transition in the law's role for righteousness. Romans calls Christ the end of law; Galatians describes law as guardian until Christ and no longer being under a guardian. The end expression and guardian image are not collapsed into one definition or an added claim about every command.

Paul's Moses citation about doing and living closely corresponds to Leviticus's command to keep and do the ordinances and judgments. Both supplied English verses say live by them. The Lord-your-God conclusion and Paul's law-righteousness introduction remain their respective framing rather than additional shared clauses.

Both use the question about ascending heaven to fetch the otherwise unavailable message. Deuteronomy concerns the accessible commandment; Romans adds its explicit Christ-down explanation and do-not-say-in-your-heart framing. Christ is not inserted into Deuteronomy as an original named figure.

The second distant-retrieval question supplies an adapted comparison: Deuteronomy asks who will cross the sea to fetch the command, whereas Romans asks who will descend the abyss and explicitly glosses bringing Christ up from the dead. Sea-crossing, descent and the Christ gloss remain distinct rather than an identical quotation.

Both say the word is near in mouth and heart. The supplied Deuteronomy also names the hands and doing it; Paul identifies the near word as the faith-word proclaimed. The extra hands/doing wording is not omitted from the target or added to Romans.

Both explicitly name the confession Jesus is Lord. Romans joins mouth confession to heart-belief in God's raising Jesus; Corinthians states the Holy Spirit condition for saying the confession. The resurrection and salvation conditions are not represented as additional words in the selected Corinthian verse.

This sentence explains the preceding heart-belief and mouth-confession condition with their righteousness/salvation relation. It is a direct internal expansion of the same two elements, not an independent second account or a specified public ceremony inferred from mouth alone.

The believe/trust-without-shame assurance repeats the Isaiah stone promise. Romans says everyone believing in Him; Isaiah's fuller declaration concerns the precious cornerstone and whoever trusts in it. The person/stone pronouns and broader target description are preserved rather than made one identical quotation.

Both explicitly set Jew and Greek within one Christ-related relation. Romans names one Lord rich toward all callers; Galatians names oneness in Christ and also slave/free and male/female. The relation and additional categories are not transferred as if the two sentences have identical contents.

The everyone-calling-upon-the-Lord's-name salvation declaration closely matches Joel. The fuller Joel verse names Zion/Jerusalem and bearers of good news called by the Lord; those clauses remain in the supplied target rather than being replaced with another edition's wording or added to Paul's short citation.

Peter recounts God's choice that Gentiles hear the gospel word through his mouth and believe, supplying a concrete proclamation/hearing/belief sequence. Romans asks how calling, believing and hearing relate to a proclaimer. Peter's particular mission is not made the only possible fulfillment or an identical wording of all three questions.

Isaiah supplies feet and good-news/peace proclamation imagery. Romans has the beautiful feet of plural announcers of good things; the supplied Isaiah uses a beauty simile and singular proclaimer and continues with Zion's salvation and divine reign. The shorter Romans wording is not lengthened with an unprinted peace clause.

Paul's Lord-who-believed-our-report citation closely matches Isaiah's question. Isaiah also asks about the Lord's arm being revealed; that further question is not inserted into Paul's shorter citation or made independent evidence that every hearer rejected the gospel.

The narrated proclamation of resurrection in Jesus is followed by many hearers believing, a concrete word/hearing/faith instance. Romans calls hearing through the word of Christ; Acts does not repeat that whole formula or imply that every hearer necessarily believed.

The earth-wide sound and words language closely matches the psalm. Its immediate setting describes heaven and firmament announcing God's glory and the sun; Paul uses the wording in his hearing argument. The comparison does not rewrite the psalm as an explicit missionary itinerary or independently verify a literal worldwide audience count.

The jealousy through a no-nation and provocation through a senseless nation correspond to the Song's divine declaration. Moses introduces the saying in Romans, but its I remains the divine speaker. The target also describes the people's earlier no-god/idol provocation, which is not added to Paul's selected clause.

Both describe unexpected divine disclosure to non-seeking or non-inquiring people. Romans pairs found with non-seekers and made-known with non-askers; Isaiah pairs manifest with non-seekers and found with non-inquirers. The actual verb/object pairings and Isaiah's further nation clause remain distinct.

The all-day outstretched hands and disobedient/contrary people closely correspond. Isaiah further names their untrue way and sins; Romans specifically introduces the saying concerning Israel. The fuller target is not silently shortened or its additional words added to the citation.

Paul's Israelite and Benjaminite self-identification has a concrete counterpart in the Philippian pedigree naming Israel and Benjamin. Romans uses his own inclusion against a total-rejection claim; the pedigree does not independently prove every Israelite's response or repeat that whole argument.

The Elijah passage shows the named prophet responding to the Lord with a complaint about Israel's abandoned allegiance, demolished altars and slain prophets. This identifies the scriptural scene Paul introduces; the God-has-not-rejected declaration belongs to Paul's argument rather than another verbatim line of that complaint.

The killed prophets, demolished altars, sole survivor and threat to Elijah's life closely correspond to his complaint. Romans reverses the altar/prophet order and omits the jealousy and sword details; those fuller words remain in the target rather than being restored to the quotation.

The seven thousand men and knees not bent to Baal correspond to the divine response. Romans says I left for Myself; the supplied Kings says You will leave and additionally names mouths not bowing to Baal. The person, tense and extra clause are preserved rather than silently harmonized.

The present remnant statement recalls the earlier Isaiah citation that a remnant of Israel will be saved. This is an internal remnant connection, while present-time grace-election language belongs here and the sea-sand multitude belongs to the earlier citation; the groups are not independently counted.

Both contrast grace with works as the basis of the saving benefit. Romans argues that grace would cease to be grace if it were from works; Ephesians names salvation through faith as God's gift rather than works. Neither supplies an absent additional works-versus-works clause to the short Romans text.

The distinction between the chosen obtaining and the rest being hardened can be compared with the earlier not-all-from-Israel-are-Israel distinction. These are related internal qualifications, not a claim that the whole people has one uniform response or identical definitions for every term.

The eyes, ears and until-this-day clause closely correspond to Deuteronomy's statement that the Lord has not given a knowing heart, seeing eyes and hearing ears. Romans has God giving stupor and organs not to perceive; the negated-giving wording is not changed into the identical whole composite quotation.

Isaiah says the Lord has made you drink a spirit of stupor and will close their eyes, also naming prophets and rulers. Romans instead says God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes not to see and ears not to hear. The drinking image, pronouns, future eye-closing and audience details remain distinct; this is another component, not one continuous verbatim passage.

The table becoming a trap, repayment and stumbling block corresponds to the psalm. Romans additionally names a snare and arranges the terms differently. Paul attributes the saying to David; the comparison retains both supplied lists rather than copying extra Romans wording into the psalm.

The eyes darkened against seeing and the back bent continually closely match the retained psalm. This is the continuation of Paul's citation, not an independent historical report about every member of the later audience or a different edition's numbering.

The stated purpose of provoking jealousy through Gentile salvation recalls the earlier cited no-nation jealousy declaration. This connects Paul's internal argument, without turning the denied final-fall purpose into his affirmation, labeling every Gentile senseless, or treating the repeated saying as an independent event.

Both questions move from a loss associated with benefit for the world toward a greater result of restoration. Wealth/fullness here and reconciliation/life-from-the-dead there remain distinct expressions. The structural parallel does not decide an unprinted resurrection timetable or make every term a strict synonym.

Galatians explicitly identifies Paul's entrusted gospel and apostleship among the nations, alongside Peter's circumcised mission. This corresponds to his Gentile-apostle self-description, without treating those emphases as a prohibition on every cross-group encounter or transferring the whole fellowship meeting into Romans.

Paul's hope of saving some of his own flesh continues the preceding prayer and desire for their salvation. Jealousy as a hoped-for means is named here, not in that prayer; some and may are preserved rather than making every kinsman already saved.

This rejection/acceptance question repeats the earlier loss/fullness pattern of benefit to the world and a greater restoration. Reconciliation and life from the dead are not rewritten as the earlier wealth language or an independently dated prediction; this is one developing argument.

Numbers commands a firstfruits portion from the dough set apart for the Lord, providing specific background to Paul's firstfruits/lump image. Paul states the whole lump's holiness and then adds root/branches; those deductions and the olive imagery are not claimed as additional Numbers sentences.

Jeremiah pictures God's planted people as a beautiful olive tree whose branches become useless under judgment; Romans pictures some olive branches broken and a wild olive grafted among them. The shared people/olive/branch image is bounded: Jeremiah does not describe the grafting or use the same broken-off wording.

The command against boasting follows the recipient's sharing the olive tree's rich root. This internal dependence explains the root-bearing-you statement without assigning an unprinted personal identity to the root or making the wild branch the tree's source.

The proposed broken-off-so-I-could-be-grafted claim is answered with unbelief, standing by faith and a warning against pride. The speaker's anticipated objection and Paul's reply remain distinct; neither becomes a separately narrated historical speech by a named Gentile.

Both warn against confidence in one's standing that neglects the danger of falling. Corinthians uses earlier examples to admonish its community; Romans names unbelief, faith and the olive-branch warning. The shared corrective does not make the images or every historical example identical.

The following kindness/severity and remain-or-be-cut-off instruction develops the warning that Gentile recipients are not automatically spared. These are connected conditional warnings within the same olive argument, not an independent claim that every addressed person has already been cut off.

Both use remaining and branch removal as warnings. Romans speaks of olive-tree participation and remaining in kindness; Jesus names Himself as vine, the Father as vinegrower and fruit-bearing/remaining in Him. The trees, roles and criteria differ rather than identifying Romans' root with an unprinted person.

The assurance that God can graft them again is developed by the following natural-versus-wild branch comparison. The if-not-remaining-in-unbelief condition and the argument's how-much-more form remain in place; ability and expectation are not rewritten as a narrated completed restoration of every branch.

The earlier wild-olive grafting supplies the actual metaphorical case used in the later how-much-more comparison for natural branches. The cultivated tree, contrary-to-nature wording and proposed return to their own tree remain Paul's imagery, not an invented modern horticultural rule.

The later partial-hardening statement corresponds to the earlier division between chosen recipients and the hardened rest. The internal qualification prevents reading this as uniform hardness of every Israelite. The until-Gentile-fullness clause belongs to this later statement and is not turned into an independently calculated date.

The deliverer and turning ungodliness from Jacob correspond to Isaiah. Romans says from Zion; the supplied Isaiah says for Zion's sake. The actual directional/purpose wording is preserved, without replacing either with a different edition's to-Zion form or treating all-Israel-saved as an extra Isaiah clause.

The this-is-My-covenant-with-them clause closely matches Isaiah. The target continues with “My spirit that is upon you” and words that will never fail from “your mouth or your offspring’s mouth”; Paul continues with removal of sins. This identifies the covenant component without representing the two whole continuations as one identical quotation.

Isaiah's when-I-remove-his-sin clause supplies the separate sin-removal comparison. Romans has their sins within its covenant citation; Isaiah names Jacob's lawlessness, his sin and removal of idolatrous objects. Person, number and surrounding conditions remain distinct rather than silently combining distant Isaiah verses into one original paragraph.

The Lord's love for the fathers and choice of their seed correspond to the beloved-for-the-fathers/election side of Paul's statement. Deuteronomy does not independently repeat the gospel-enemy side, and the contrast does not erase either of Paul's stated relations.

The oracle asks whether God speaks without acting and its blessing speaker declares he will not reverse the blessing. This is specific fidelity/non-reversal background for God's irrevocable gifts and calling, with different speakers and objects; the human I-will-bless clause is not silently reassigned as God's own first-person sentence.

Both contrast former disobedience with present divine mercy. Romans addresses you and connects that mercy with their disobedience; Titus speaks of we once being disobedient and salvation by God's mercy. The pronouns, intergroup relation and washing/Spirit-renewal explanation remain particular to each passage.

The preceding Gentile disobedience-to-mercy case supplies the reciprocal pattern for the hope of mercy stated here. The repeated now and the may-receive purpose are preserved rather than changed into permanent collective exclusion or a claim that all have already received mercy.

Both use confinement under wrong as the setting for a saving benefit. Romans names God confining all in disobedience for mercy on all; Galatians names Scripture confining everything under sin so the faith-promise may be given to believers. Agents, objects and stated beneficiaries are not collapsed into identical wording.

Zophar asks about finding the Lord's trace and the limits of what the Almighty made; Paul marvels at unsearchable judgments and untraceable ways. The divine-knowledge/depth comparison does not endorse Zophar's surrounding accusation about Job's sins or turn his question into Paul's identical doxology.

The Lord's mind and counselor questions closely match Isaiah. Romans joins its questions with or, while Isaiah adds to-instruct-Him after the counselor question. The comparison retains the shorter citation without adding the target's final purpose phrase.

Elihu asks what a righteous person gives God or what He receives from that person's hand; Paul asks who gave first so that repayment is owed. These are related giving-to-God questions, not a verbatim quotation: first-giving and repayment are not inserted into the selected Job text.

Romans gives from/through/to-Him all-things praise. Corinthians explicitly names one God the Father from whom are all things and we for Him, and one Lord Jesus through whom are all things and we through Him. The origin/agency language corresponds without turning the target's distinct references to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ into one identical formula.

Both use offerings acceptable to God for the faithful: Romans presents living bodies as holy sacrifice and rational worship; Peter describes spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ within a living-stone priesthood image. The bodies, stones and sacrifice descriptions remain distinct, without demanding literal bodily killing.

Both connect transformed conduct with renewal of the mind. Romans adds discerning God's good, pleasing and perfect will; Ephesians places renewed spirit-of-the-mind language within putting off the old and putting on the new human being. The clothing image and the mind's spirit are not silently replaced with an identical explicit Holy Spirit statement.

Romans grounds sober self-estimation in God's apportioning a measure of faith; Corinthians challenges boasting over what was received. Both oppose inflated self-regard by reference to received provision, without equating every gift with the particular measure-of-faith expression.

Both use one body with many parts to explain differentiated functions. Corinthians develops the image with foot, hand, ear and eye and God's placement of parts; those examples and its baptism clause are not inserted into Romans as identical wording.

Both explicitly describe the community as Christ's body and its people as members. Romans adds belonging to one another; Corinthians addresses its own community as individual members. The communities and particular clauses remain distinct.

Both place differing gifts within a common divine provision and include prophecy. Romans speaks of grace and the proportion of faith; Corinthians names the Spirit's distribution as He wills and gives its own gift list. The lists, named agents and criteria are not made identical.

Both require received gifts to be exercised in service, with speech and service distinguished in Peter. Romans specifically names teaching; Peter's speaking-as-words-from-God language is not treated as a verbatim description of every teacher or the same list of offices.

Romans separately commends generous sharing and cheerful mercy; Corinthians calls for willing giving and says God loves a cheerful giver. The practical generosity and cheerfulness correspond, while Romans' cheerfulness belongs grammatically to mercy rather than being silently moved to its giving clause.

Romans commands love without hypocrisy; Peter calls for sincere brotherly love and earnest mutual love from a pure heart. The related descriptions retain their different actual wording; Romans' adjoining evil/good commands are not added to Peter's selected statement.

Romans joins abhorring evil with clinging to good; Thessalonians pairs holding to good with abstention from evil. The paired moral directions correspond, while Thessalonians' testing command and Romans' unhypocritical-love clause retain their own places.

Both link love within the brotherhood with honoring others. Romans emphasizes mutual devotion and taking the lead in honor; Peter separately names honoring everyone, loving the brotherhood, fearing God and honoring the king. The recipient scopes and extra commands are not collapsed.

The fervent-in-spirit description of Apollos provides a narrative comparison for the exhortation to be fervent in spirit while serving the Lord. His stated instruction and limited baptism knowledge remain his own circumstances, not proof that every fervent person has complete knowledge.

Both join rejoicing with persistent prayer. Romans additionally locates rejoicing in hope and commands endurance in affliction; Thessalonians adds thanksgiving. These are related exhortations, not a claim that all surrounding clauses are identical.

The hospitality command has a close counterpart in Hebrews' instruction not to forget hospitality. Hebrews adds the unrecognized-angel illustration; that is not made an identity for every guest or an extra clause of Romans' support for the saints.

Both command a positive response to hostility, explicitly blessing rather than retaliation. Romans names persecutors and forbids cursing; Luke names enemies, haters, cursers and mistreaters with its own commands. The different hostile actions and commands remain distinct.

Shared rejoicing and sorrow correspond to the body image in which all members suffer together and rejoice when one is honored. Romans names rejoicers and mourners, while Corinthians names members, suffering and honor; this is not an identical list of circumstances.

Proverbs warns against being prudent in one's own estimation; Romans warns against being wise in one's own eyes. The self-estimation warning is close, with different wording; Proverbs adds fearing God and turning from evil, while Romans adds mutual-mindedness and association with the lowly.

Both explicitly prohibit repaying evil for evil. Thessalonians adds pursuit of good toward one another and everyone; Romans adds taking thought for honorable conduct before all people. The shared prohibition does not replace the respective positive clauses.

Romans commands taking thought for what is honorable before everyone; Corinthians describes taking care to do what is honorable before the Lord and people in administering a gift. The public-integrity concern connects the exhortation and the concrete collection arrangement.

Both urge peace with all people. Romans retains its if-possible and as-far-as-depends-on-you qualifications; Hebrews joins peace to holiness. Neither set of additional clauses is silently substituted for the other.

Paul places the Lord's repayment declaration after forbidding personal vengeance. The supplied Deuteronomy says in the day of vengeance I will repay, whereas Romans says vengeance is Mine, I will repay. The shared divine repayment is preserved without changing the target's opening clause or making it a command for personal revenge.

Both repeat the divine vengeance-and-repayment declaration. Hebrews joins it to the Lord's judging His people; Romans uses it to prohibit personal revenge. The different surrounding applications remain distinct, without converting the warning into a command for human retaliation.

The commands to feed a hungry enemy and give drink, followed by the coals-of-fire image, closely match Proverbs. The target additionally promises the Lord's repayment with good things. That clause stays in Proverbs, and no unprinted ritual, material identity or motive is assigned to the coals image.

Conquering evil with good corresponds to Peter's prohibition of evil-for-evil and insult-for-insult repayment and command to bless instead. The positive counter-response is shared, with different metaphors and Peter's inheritance-of-blessing explanation not inserted into Romans.
